item.title: Arizona man arrested after allegedly emailing White House bomb threat to Tucson news station
item.description: Jacob Aaron Hicks allegedly emailed a Tucson news station claiming an imminent bomb strike against the White House, prompting an FBI investigation.
item.content:encoded:
An Arizona man was arrested Wednesday after allegedly sending an email threatening to carry out bombings at the White House and other locations in Washington, D.C., federal officials said.

Jacob Aaron Hicks, 46, of Tucson, was charged with making an interstate threat to injure, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Arizona announced.

According to the criminal complaint, Hicks allegedly emailed a local Tucson television station on Sept. 23, claiming that there would be an "imminent bomb strike against the White House and other locations in Washington, D.C."

After receiving the email, the station alerted law enforcement, prompting an investigation into the threat.

FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED FOR ALLEGEDLY THREATENING TO KILL TRUMP, RUBIO AND BONDI

Authorities said they later identified Hicks as the alleged sender of the email.

"We must take threats of violence like this one seriously," U.S. Attorney Timothy Courchaine said in a statement.

"I am grateful to our local news station for referring this threat to law enforcement, and to the FBI for addressing the situation quickly, professionally, and with the level of commitment it required," Courchaine added.

According to federal officials, investigators also discovered additional email drafts in the account linked to Hicks.

OHIO MAN CHARGED OVER GRAPHIC THREATS TO KILL TRUMP, BEHEAD GOP LAWMAKER

Officials said the drafts, also dated Sept. 23, were addressed to other news organizations and contained similar threats involving the White House and other locations in Washington, D.C.

The FBI is leading the investigation with assistance from the U.S. Secret Service.

FBI Phoenix Special Agent in Charge Rebecca Day credited the news station for alerting authorities to the threat.

"We appreciate the community partner who reported the threat to law enforcement. Cooperation and partnership are essential to protecting the American people," Day said.

The U.S. Attorney's Office said Hicks made his initial appearance in federal court Thursday.

item.title: Logan Federico’s dad says criminals have become 'more important' than victims, pushes repeat offender registry
item.description: Stephen Federico urged federal lawmakers to pass Logan's Law, which would include a violent crime registry bill, at a South Carolina roundtable with AG Todd Blanche.
item.content:encoded:
The father of Logan Federico, a 22-year-old college student murdered during a home break-in, is demanding federal lawmakers close legal loopholes that allow career criminals back on the street.

Stephen Federico is championing "Logan’s Law," a legislative proposal that would mandate a public database for repeat violent offenders, force cross-county and interstate communication and hold prosecutors accountable when handling habitual criminals.

The bill aims to eliminate systemic blind spots that allowed Logan's accused killer, Alexander Dickey, to avoid long-term confinement despite a lengthy record.

ONE YEAR AFTER IRYNA ZARUTSKA MURDER, VIOLENT CRIMES FUEL NORTH CAROLINA PUBLIC SAFETY DEBATE

"This was preventable. And d-----, I'm not going to save just one more life," Federico said Thursday during a South Carolina roundtable on crime reduction attended by U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche. "I'm going to save thousands."

Federico pointed to broader systemic breakdowns, comparing domestic criminal justice failures to immigration enforcement gaps.

TEEN'S TRAGIC KILLING BY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT BECOMES FLASHPOINT IN BATTLE FOR CONTROL OF CONGRESS

"We are fighting 15 million that crossed our borders — some horrific criminals, some not," he added. "Now we're also fighting the constant felon. How are we supposed to win without Logan's Law?"

Introduced by U.S. Rep. Russell Fry, R-S.C., and late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., Logan's Law has not yet formally come to the floor in either the House or the Senate.

LINDSEY GRAHAM, SOUTH CAROLINA SENATOR WHO ROSE FROM SMALL-TOWN ROOTS TO GOP POWER BROKER, DIES AT 71

"Common sense works. Common sense is easy," Fry said, comparing the proposed legislation to existing public registries. "We have a sexual abuse registry that is publicly searchable. This is for violent crimes. It's the same concept."

Attorney General Blanche urged lawmakers to move swiftly.

"It took a tragedy to push it to the forefront," Blanche said. "But that's OK. I think the worst thing we could do is not act."

Blanche expressed hope for bipartisan support, adding, "I don't think it's a controversial issue. ... I know President Trump supports it."

BIDEN ADMIN RELEASED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF FATALLY STABBING FAIRFAX COUNTY MOTHER

Logan Federico, a North Carolina college student, was staying with friends at a South Carolina home on May 3, 2025, when Dickey allegedly broke in.

According to Columbia police, Dickey drove a stolen vehicle into the neighborhood, broke into one home to steal vehicle keys and a gun and then forced his way into the house where Federico was staying.

Inside, Dickey allegedly stole credit cards and fatally shot Federico. Her father noted that she was awake during the intrusion.

HOUSE DEMOCRAT BLASTED AFTER EARLY RELEASE LAW FREED INMATES LATER CHARGED WITH MURDER

"He didn't kill our daughter for a debit card," Federico said. "She was the only one awake who could identify him. He killed a witness."

Dickey had an extensive criminal record dating back to 2013, including convictions for breaking and entering, burglary, grand larceny, strong-arm robbery, possession of a stolen vehicle and resisting arrest. Critics and authorities argue he slipped through the cracks of a lenient justice system.

"What we do as a society right now is make the criminal more important than the innocent," Federico said, criticizing progressive policies such as reduced sentencing and no-cash bail. "We have turned the page. We are the underdogs."

Fox News' David Spunt contributed to this report.

item.title: Guinness brewery that welcomed 2 million visitors closing its doors for good
item.description: One of America's two Guinness breweries is closing, leaving 174 Aramark employees out of work. The brewery's last day open to the public will be Nov. 1.
item.content:encoded:
The Guinness Open Gate Brewery in Halethorpe, Maryland, just outside Baltimore, will soon close, leaving the iconic Irish beer brand's Chicago brewery as its only U.S. location.

Nov. 1 will mark the brewery's final day open to the public, leaving 174 Aramark employees out of work, according to a notice filed with the Maryland Department of Labor Oct. 1.

The move comes amid a $1 billion restructuring plan at Diageo, Guinness' parent company.

BREWERY THAT OFFERED FREE BEER WHEN TRUMP DIES FACES POSSIBLE CLOSURE AFTER STATE REVOKES ALCOHOL PERMITS

Some teams at Diageo are losing 20% to 30% of their staff, Reuters reported in July.

"This decision follows a careful review of our operations and long-term business priorities," a Diageo spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "It is not a reflection of the passion, talent or dedication of our team, nor of the support we have received from consumers and the Baltimore community since we opened our doors in 2018."

Since opening in 2018, the Guinness Open Gate Brewery has welcomed more than 2 million visitors, according to a post on its Facebook page.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

The brewery was the first to open in the U.S. since the Irish beer maker's previous brewery in New York closed in 1954, FOX Business reported at the time.

"It's obviously a shame to see the Guinness brewery close in Maryland," said Derek Brown of Drink Company, a Washington, D.C.-based hospitality consulting and events company.

"However, I'm not surprised in the sense that their core product remains Guinness, and now Guinness Zero," Brown told Fox News Digital. "The brewery focused on experimental products, which are interesting in themselves, but not necessarily primary drivers of Guinness' business."

The experimental portion of the brewery allowed guests to concoct their own brews, and more than 700 beers were created over the years, according to the brewery's Facebook post.

But changing trends in alcohol consumption likely played a role in the decision, industry experts say.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

New research shows that U.S. alcohol use has declined for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, Fox News Digital recently reported.

More Americans are also alternating between alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages — a practice known as "zebra striping" — partly contributing to the decline, according to experts.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Our immediate focus is supporting affected colleagues through this transition," a Diageo spokesperson said. "We are committed to treating our team members with respect and providing resources and assistance to help them navigate the change."

The spokesperson added that Guinness "remains one of our most important brands, and we are committed to investing in its long-term growth and success. While our Baltimore brewery will close, our commitment to bringing Guinness to consumers around the world remains as strong as ever."

item.title: Caitlin Clark's Fever set a TV ratings bar the WNBA semifinal openers could not come close to reaching
item.description: Indiana Fever regular-season games averaged 2.32 million viewers on major networks, more than double Sunday's WNBA semifinal openers on ABC and NBC.
item.content:encoded:
The Indiana Fever's regular-season games on major broadcast networks averaged more than twice the audience of the WNBA semifinal openers on Oct. 4.

And those playoff games were on ABC and NBC.

An OutKick review of Indiana's 10 regular-season games on ABC, CBS and NBC found an average audience of approximately 2.32 million viewers. The two semifinal openers averaged about 1.16 million.

CAITLIN CLARK SENDS WNBA ALL-STAR RATINGS SOARING AS 3-POINT CONTEST AUDIENCE FALLS WITHOUT HER

That gave Indiana an average audience approximately 100% larger, a difference of nearly 1.16 million viewers per game.

New York–Atlanta's Game 1 averaged 1.2 million viewers on ABC, ESPN told OutKick. Las Vegas–Golden State averaged 1.12 million on NBC and Peacock, according to figures NBC supplied to OutKick.

Just one Sunday earlier, Indiana's first-round opener against Las Vegas averaged 2.11 million viewers on ABC. That Sept. 27 game also aired opposite the NFL, yet drew approximately 76% more viewers than New York–Atlanta's semifinal opener on the same network a week later.

The stakes went up, but the audience went down.

That's a pretty good answer to anyone still wondering how much Caitlin Clark means to the WNBA's television business.

The 2.32 million average covers four Fever games on ABC, four on CBS and two on NBC, using reported audiences from the regular season. The NBC figures include Peacock, just as the Aces–Valkyries playoff figure does.

Seven of those 10 Fever games exceeded two million viewers. Every one of the 10 drew a larger audience than either semifinal opener.

The smallest was Indiana's May 30 game at Portland on CBS, which Sports Media Watch reported at nearly 1.3 million. Clark had one of her worst games of the season, scoring just 6 points on 1-for-7 shooting, and the Fever trailed by as many as 26 points.

Think about that, though. A regular-season game against Portland in May, where Clark played just 22 minutes in a blowout loss, drew more viewers than either game to open the WNBA semifinals in October.

WNBA WANTS A BIGGER STORY THAN CAITLIN CLARK, BUT TV RATINGS KEEP POINTING BACK TO HER

At the other end, Indiana's Aug. 23 game against Chicago averaged 3.31 million viewers on NBC and Peacock. Its July 12 game against Las Vegas drew 2.64 million on those same platforms.

New York offers another useful comparison. The Liberty's two regular-season meetings with Indiana on CBS each drew over 2.5 million viewers. Sunday's Liberty–Dream semifinal opener drew 1.2 million on ABC.

Angel Reese, who now plays for Atlanta, famously insisted in 2024 that people watch women's basketball "because of me too."

Well, New York facing Clark's Fever in the regular season drew more than twice the audience of New York facing Reese's Dream in the final four. The numbers show that Reese isn't much of a television draw, as Dream playoff games are right in line with the other non-Clark games and, in some cases, actually worse.

Atlanta's first-round clincher averaged 1.2 million viewers on ESPN, below the 1.4 million for Dallas–Golden State on the same network that night.

This isn't to say that this is bad news for the WNBA because it isn't. Before Clark arrived in 2024, the league hadn't had a game average one million viewers since 2008. Consistently clearing that mark represents real progress.

WNBA MEDIA RIGHTS DEAL BALLOONS PAST $3 BILLION AFTER ADDING NEW BROADCAST PARTNERS TO 11-YEAR PORTFOLIO

Plus, the two semifinal openers averaged around 10% more viewers than last year's pair. Sports Media Watch ranked them second and third among semifinal Game 1 audiences since the league adopted its current semifinal format in 2016.

The only opener ahead of them? Last year's Fever–Aces game, which drew 1.4 million on ABC even with Clark sidelined by injury.

That's encouraging for the league, and another reminder of the audience Indiana has built. Even during this year's regular season, the Fever drew 1.57 million against Los Angeles on CBS on June 27 without Clark playing.

There is an audience for the Fever beyond simply checking whether Clark is in uniform that day. The WNBA would benefit enormously from building that kind of interest around more of its teams.

As I reported earlier this week, even Indiana's least-watched first-round game, its 1.42 million-viewer appearance on Prime Video, outdrew every non-Fever first-round game. That streaming-exclusive audience also exceeded both semifinal openers on broadcast television.

Fans found the Fever wherever their games aired. The remaining teams now have the opportunity to give those viewers a reason to keep watching.

I'll be interested to see whether the audiences build as the series progress.

For now, though, the remaining teams are trying to match numbers the Fever were putting up in May.

item.title: Tyreek Hill denies most abuse claims but admits to shoving wife into wall in explosive testimony
item.description: Tyreek Hill admitted to pushing Lakeeta Vaccaro Hill into a wall and threatening her but denied multiple other battery allegations on the witness stand.
item.content:encoded:
Free agent NFL wide receiver Tyreek Hill took the witness stand in his divorce and battery civil case in Miami on Thursday, and it was as explosive as his speed and play-making ability on the field.

During approximately two hours of testimony, Hill ...

…Claimed his 18-month marriage to Lakeeta Vaccaro Hill was punctuated by arguments about her refusal to sign a post-nuptial agreement, her stealing between $60,000-$100,000 a month from a family account, her insistence his family leave their sprawling Broward County estate, and occasionally him flirting with other women.

TYREEK HILL'S NFL RETURN SEEMED IMMINENT AND THEN HIS DIVORCE TRIAL BEGAN WITH DOMESTIC ABUSE ALLEGATIONS

Hill, 32, denied he ever punched Vaccaro's stomach while she was pregnant, twisted her breasts, pulled out her hair, shoved a lit blunt into her face, or left her on the side of a road – which Vaccaro claimed on the witness stand earlier this week.

But Hill did admit to throwing Vaccaro up against a wall of their Sunny Isle, Florida condo, creating a hole in the structure. He did admit to threatening her by saying he knew people who could hurt her.

And he did apologize for cursing out both Vaccaro and her mother – a rant that is on tape.

That's not all.

Hill accused Vaccaro of indirectly being responsible for causing the fire that burned down their home in Broward County. And he also accused her of causing him to play worse once they got married because of the constant fighting.

"I felt like If you look at my career before and my career after I got married it was, like, trending down," he testified. "And it was, like, bad. I was like, man, am I really putting this product on the field? Do I really look that bad? It was hard."

Hill's testimony wrapped up at 5:41 p.m. but he is scheduled back on the witness stand on Friday because Thursday's session was all direct testimony. Vaccaro's attorney will have a chance for redirect on Friday.

So, a lot to unpack here.

Hill and Vaccaro were married in November 2021, but there was no prenuptial or post-nuptial agreement. And that became one of the pillars of their constant fighting during the 18-month marriage.

"Obviously, the postnup is definitely one of the constant arguments and then finances," Hill said. "I think that's a very important topic that has to be explored through this whole entire thing.

"Then money getting stolen, and the mother of my kids. I would literally have conversations with the mothers of my [other] kids and she would be, 'You're doing, X, Y, Z with them. You're being intimate with them.

"Those were the primary arguments."

Hill admitted he and Vaccaro discussed the postnuptial seemingly countless times. And often those ended in arguments. Hill accused Vaccaro of marrying him because of her interest in his money.

It began with Vaccaro taking $10,000 one time before their marriage. And then, he testified, the sums got larger after the marriage.

"I was like, babe, why you stealing money?" Hill testified. "All you have to do is say, 'help me out.' She stole money then. She stole money during the marriage while getting what she was already getting, which she was getting $15K.

"Then she was taking around $60K a month and I would see that and it'd be, 'You're giving this person this and that person that.'"

Hill also said Vaccaro's monthly take at one point was $100,000 in one month.

He also testified that Vaccaro didn't like his family around their baby girl. But when the couple's home burned, and they moved to the swank Porsche Design Tower in Miami, she moved her mom in.

"It was one of those where I said have your mom come down for a little bit to help you out at the beginning of the pregnancy," Hill said. "I didn't know she was going to come down and stay for two years."

The couple split but agreed to get counseling. During one of those sessions, Hill said, both agreed many of their conversations "were getting out of hand."

That included allegations by Vaccaro that Hill was physically abusive on at least eight different times. Hill denied all those happened except one time he came home to pack clothes and leave.

"As I'm getting my clothes, I feel somebody brush up behind me," Hill said. "And that person brushing up behind me is my wife, and I'm like, hold on, hold on ... That continued for like five minutes.

"I told her don't you ever touch me again in your life. I pushed her against the wall. And I tried to force her to get off me. I created a hole in the wall, trying to force her to get off me that night."

Hill testified that despite pushing his wife into a wall, he and her "got physically intimate that night." But later he had remorse and decided he definitely wanted a divorce.

"I didn't want to be that in front of my daughter," he said. "I felt embarrassed, you know what I'm saying?"

Hill also testified about a fateful car ride home in May 2024 in which Vaccaro claims he shoved her into a car door, threw her shoe out of the car and drank.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Hill admitted to drinking socially. And he also admitted he warned his wife about what might happen to her if he wanted to hurt her.

"I did, I did make statements about she wasn't safe," Hill said. "I did make statements about me being able to get people to hurt her. Like now, looking back, I wish I could have handled that situation better.

"I wish I could have talked to my wife better. I wish I could take it all back."

Hill also testified that his grandmother and sister "wanted to do some things to [Vaccaro] but knew she was, in Hill's words, "the love of my life."

item.title: Pennsylvania school district unveils plans for gender-neutral ‘universal toilet rooms’
item.description: Strath Haven High School's $76 million renovation includes "universal toilet rooms" on every floor, with cameras and walled-off stalls to curb loitering.
item.content:encoded:
A Pennsylvania high school is planning to build gender-neutral bathroom facilities as part of a massive renovation project estimated to cost approximately $76 million, according to architectural plans presented to the local school board.

The Wallingford-Swarthmore School District's Sept. 15 schematic design presentation for Strath Haven High School includes plans for "universal toilet rooms" on multiple floors of the building, along with a rendering showing individual bathroom stalls and a shared sink area.

The proposed bathroom overhaul is part of a broader renovation that includes new science classrooms, infrastructure improvements and expanded academic space. 

The district's own student newspaper, The Panther Press, reported that the project would replace existing gendered bathrooms with larger universal facilities on each floor.

WEST VIRGINIA PRINCIPAL SUSPENDED AFTER RECORDING DEVICES FOUND IN GIRLS’ LOCKER ROOMS

Architectural plans presented to the Wallingford-Swarthmore School District in September show proposed "universal toilet rooms" on all four floors of Strath Haven High School as part of a $76 million renovation proposal.

"The plan also includes a complete reconstruction of the building’s bathrooms," the Panther Press reported Sept. 29. "In place of the current gendered bathrooms, the plan proposes to create a new and larger universal gender-neutral bathroom on each floor. The model also includes a separate faculty toilet only accessible from the hallway."

The student newspaper reported that the architect for the plan, Mike Kelly of Kelly Clough Baker and Associates, said that the new bathrooms would allow cameras inside while the stalls are designed to be completely walled off and hidden from the cameras.

The outlet reported that Kelly said this would assist the administration’s control of the bathrooms and address loitering in the bathroom.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OPENS FOUR TITLE IX INVESTIGATIONS INTO MICHIGAN AND NORTH CAROLINA SCHOOL DISTRICTS

"We’ve seen this in a lot of schools really cutting down on behavior issues that happen in restrooms," Kelly said.

The Wallingford-Swarthmore School District confirmed to Fox News Digital that "the district has developed plans to create universal toilet rooms for students."

"As has been the case in a growing number of middle and high schools, this design was selected to enhance student privacy, safety and supervision," the spokesperson said. 

"Each student will have access to an acoustically separated, fully enclosed private toilet room, providing a level of privacy that exceeds what is available in a traditional school restroom configuration. The Wallingford-Swarthmore Board of School Directors recently approved the schematic design as part of the Strath Haven High School renovation project.

DAD OF THIRD-GRADE GIRL IN MASSACHUSETTS ALLEGEDLY BARGED IN ON BY TRANS STUDENT IN BATHROOM CALLS FOR ACTION

"Each toilet room will be fully enclosed with floor-to-ceiling walls and doors and will be acoustically separated from adjacent rooms. In addition, each room will be equipped with vape detection technology and fire alarm devices. Cameras will monitor entry and exit areas outside the bathrooms, providing enhanced supervision while maintaining privacy within the individual rooms."

The spokesperson added that some traditional restroom layouts in the existing school will remain, and the Board of School Directors approved a project budget capped at $70 million, with most of the funding dedicated to upgrading and renovating the existing school’s infrastructure.

The district said additional details on costs and budget allocations are available in its publicly posted schematic design presentation.

item.title: Anti-Zuckerberg movie 'The Social Reckoning' takes critical heat on both sides of political aisle
item.description: Aaron Sorkin's "The Social Reckoning" faced blistering critiques from both conservatives and liberals and sits at 59% on Rotten Tomatoes.
item.content:encoded:
"The Social Reckoning," the follow-up to the 2010 hit "The Social Network," is facing blistering critiques from both sides of the political spectrum alongside lukewarm reviews from critics, with some reviewers sharply criticizing the film's political messaging and its handling of Facebook's role in American politics.

"The Social Network" focused on the creation of Facebook and the legal battle over its ownership, earning three Oscars, including for screenwriter Aaron Sorkin, and a 96% positive rating on review-aggregation website Rotten Tomatoes. 

It's more political follow-up, "The Social Reckoning," written and directed by Sorkin, has received a more mixed response, with a 61% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes as of Thursday evening.

DAVID MARCUS: WOKE 1.0 IS WHY ENTERTAINERS NEEDED OUR SECRET CONSERVATIVE CLUB

Earlier this year, a trailer debuted showing Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg (played by Jeremy Strong) being questioned by a character played by comedian Bill Burr. In the scene, Zuckerberg defends online free speech and argues that users are responsible for their own behavior. Burr’s character vigorously challenges him. 

Sorkin published an open letter in 2019 criticizing Zuckerberg’s management of the platform.

OutKick writer Ian Miller was one of several conservative critics who mocked the trailer as tone-deaf, replying, "It is the most Hollywood thing ever to desperately try and convince everyone that the guy making complete sense is the bad guy and the one demanding authoritarian ideological enforcement is the good guy."

Film critics were also sharply critical. The Globe and Mail film critic Barry Hertz tweeted that the film was "one of the most insipid, ugly, flat films of the year — an insufferably sanctimonious fantasia of blue-state Boomers." 

In his actual review, he argued that the movie is counterproductive in that it "will turn even the most hardcore Facebook hater into a true-blue Facebook believer — the film is just that magnificently, unbelievably, despicably bad."

Variety said it badly missed the original's director David Fincher and "already feels behind the curve," while Wired magazine’s review described the new film as one that "already feels irrelevant."

Wired noted that the movie opens with the DUI arrest of a woman who directs racist, right-wing insults at police officers and is arrested for threatening to kill one of them. When the video goes viral, a Facebook whistleblower recognizes the woman as a former liberal acquaintance from her Pilates class.

The film's climax, as noted by Wired, is the Jan. 6, 2021, capitol riot, "the horrors of which are blamed in part on Facebook’s failure to either get a handle on election fraud conspiracy theories or remove Donald Trump’s account as he stoked such inflammatory falsehoods."

"Now, halfway into Trump’s second term, is it all that much of a revelation that he and his movement are emboldened by the complicity of tech oligarchs, who openly backed him in 2024?" the outlet asked.

CHRIS MURPHY CALLS FOR 'REGULATING THE INTERNET' SO PEOPLE WON'T FALL FOR A 'DEMAGOGUE LIKE DONALD TRUMP'

Journalist and film critic Stephen Silver described the movie as "an old-man-yells-at-cloud treatment of Facebook." Silver wrote that Sorkin essentially argues Facebook was not censorious enough in the 2010s and that the government should now step in by reforming Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, a federal law that generally shields online platforms from liability for content posted by users.

"No, I don’t buy that Facebook is primarily responsible for American political extremism, or for January 6," Silver wrote, arguing that individuals remain responsible for their own actions online.

SFGate's Lindsey Bahr wrote that while certain political aspects hit the mark, the movie falls far short of its predecessor: "It is unfortunate for ‘The Social Reckoning’ that ‘The Social Network’ exists." 

IndieWire was even harsher, panning its script and performances.

The BBC's reviewer gave it two out of five stars, calling it unlikely to influence anyone, while The Guardian in a mixed review dismissed it as a "film which doesn’t reckon with the future we’re living in."

Even some reviews rated as positive on Rotten Tomatoes were tepid in their assessments. A review from The Seattle Times said it moved "snappily" but was still a "pale imitation" of "The Social Network."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Media Research Center President David Bozell commented on the film's political messaging to Fox News Digital.

"It says everything you need to know about Aaron Sorkin and the Hollywood elite that they would make a movie suggesting Big Tech’s real failure was not censoring conservatives enough," Bozell said.

"The Media Research Center spent years exposing how Facebook suppressed conservative voices, and we were right to do it," he continued. "Mark Zuckerberg eventually acknowledged Meta’s past censorship abuses and took meaningful steps to move the company back toward a more open platform. Meta is far from perfect, but Zuckerberg deserves some credit for redirecting it away from the censorship monster it had become.

"Hollywood seems determined to fight yesterday’s battle even as Zuckerberg has moved on from it," Bozell added. "Americans have had enough of government-imposed censorship, ideological gatekeeping and Big Tech deciding which political views they are allowed to hear."

Among the more positive reviews of the movie came from the San Francisco Chronicle, praising it as a "stirring journalistic thriller."

item.title: Woman, 87, dies after being carried from home of 70 years on stretcher during eviction in Spain
item.description: Maricarmen Abascal's eviction from her Madrid apartment of 70 years sparked massive protests, and her death has deepened Spain's housing crisis.
item.content:encoded:
The death of an 87-year-old woman who was evicted from her longtime home has intensified a political crisis in Spain, where nationwide protests over soaring housing costs have helped force an early election.

María del Carmen Abascal, known as "Maricarmen," died Wednesday after being hospitalized following her eviction from a Madrid apartment where she had lived for seven decades, according to The Associated Press.

Her death came just days after Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for Nov. 29 after his government's failure to pass emergency housing measures through Parliament.

The controversy has put renewed pressure on Sánchez's Socialist Party as Spain grapples with widespread frustration over rising rents and housing affordability.

SPANISH OPPOSITION LEADER CALLS PRIME MINISTER A ‘TRAITOR’ OVER CEUTA MIGRANT CRISIS

At the center of the uproar was Abascal's Sept. 23 eviction, which drew national attention after images showed the elderly woman, who used a wheelchair, being carried from her apartment on a stretcher.

Police had cordoned off the street and removed demonstrators who attempted to stop the eviction.

The images sparked demonstrations in Madrid and other Spanish cities, turning Abascal into a symbol of the country's housing crisis.

The real estate company responsible for her eviction had sought to lease the apartment at a substantially higher price, according to the AP.

ANGRY LOCALS BLOCK FAMOUS BEACH AS MASS TOURISM PROTESTS ESCALATE AT VACATION HOT SPOT

Facing mounting public pressure, the company eventually agreed to allow Abascal to return to her home. She died before she could move back.

Her cause of death has not been disclosed.

After news of her death, demonstrators gathered outside Spain's Parliament and in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square, where some observed a minute of silence.

Protesters also chanted, "Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!"

TENS OF THOUSANDS FLOOD STREETS TO PROTEST SPAIN BORDER CRISIS

Sánchez offered condolences in a statement on X.

"All my love to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," he wrote. "A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace."

Conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also expressed condolences and urged political leaders not to use the woman's death for political gain.

"No campaign, no party, no use for political advantage," he wrote. "When faced with the death of a person, we must only show respect."

Abascal's eviction and death have become a rallying point for housing activists demanding changes to Spain's rental policies as the country prepares for its November election.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Human vs ChatGPT NFL Week 5 betting picks: AI wins a round, but the human still leads the season
item.description: ChatGPT finally beat the human analyst for a week, but the human still leads the season race as their NFL Week 5 cards collide over the 49ers and Seahawks.
item.content:encoded:
It finally happened. The robot beat me.

After three straight weeks of me earning more units in NFL betting than ChatGPT, GPT edged me out in Week 4 by going 3-2 against my 2-2-1. Not only that, but it beat me head-to-head in both games where we took opposite sides.

Suddenly, the robot apocalypse seems more realistic than ever. Please forgive me, humanity.

item.title: Columbia University faces backlash over serving 'October 7th blush sauce' on campus menu
item.description: Columbia University's dining hall menu listed "October 7th" next to "blush sauce" on the third anniversary of the Hamas attack, sparking immediate backlash.
item.content:encoded:
Columbia University faced backlash after a campus dining menu appeared to advertise "October 7th Blush Sauce" on the third anniversary of the deadly Hamas terror attacks Wednesday.

The menu was publicized by Israeli newspaper Haaretz correspondent Simone Saidmehr, who shared an image of it, which placed "October 7th" next to "Blush Sauce." Many comments took the image as a reference to the approximately 1,200 victims of the terror attacks.

However, in a comment to Fox News Digital, Vicki Dunn, assistant vice president of Columbia Dining, insisted the menu printing was an "unfortunate mistake" and was corrected shortly after it was discovered.

THREE COLUMBIA UNIVERSITY ADMINISTRATORS RESIGN AFTER 'ANTISEMITIC TROPES' FOUND IN TEXT MESSAGES

"This was an unfortunate mistake and was not intended as a reference to the events of October 7," Dunn said. "The blush sauce was scheduled to be served, and when that information was copied into the menu template, the date was accidentally left in. Our staff took the signs down as soon as the mistake was identified. We are sorry for the confusion and concern this caused."

"Moving forward, Columbia Dining will also have a team member review all menus before they are posted," she added.

Columbia University released a similar statement on X in response to Saidmehr's original post.

COLUMBIA UNIVERSITY 'OCCUPIERS' WHO HELD STAFF HOSTAGE HAVE DISCIPLINE OVERTURNED BY NY JUDGE

"This was a mistake, not a reference to the events of October 7. The date was accidentally left in when the day’s meal information was copied into the menu template. The signs were removed as soon as the error was caught, and we’re sorry for the concern and confusion this caused," Columbia's X post read.

Columbia University was one of several college campuses that faced protest encampments and riots in the wake of the Oct. 7 attacks three years ago. As a result, the university faced multiple federal civil rights investigations based on claims that it failed to protect Jewish students.

By July 2025, the Trump administration secured a $221 million settlement from Columbia University for alleged discriminatory practices as well as to settle claims of antisemitic employment discrimination against Jewish faculty.

ANTI-ISRAEL PROTESTERS LABEL MAMDANI A 'TRAITOR,' ACCUSE HIM OF 'GENOCIDE' OUTSIDE OCT 7 VIGIL

However, the New York university continued to be the site of anti-Israel activism. Several anti-Israel demonstrators from the Columbia Intifada also descended on school Wednesday afternoon. 

Columbia University has previously told Fox News Digital that the Columbia Intifada is not officially associated with the Ivy League school.

item.title: Pentagon confirms Fort Hood terrorist's firing squad execution will be livestreamed: 'Details will follow'
item.description: The Pentagon confirms Fort Hood terrorist Nidal Hasan's firing squad execution will be livestreamed, according to a Pentagon official.
item.content:encoded:
The Pentagon confirmed to Fox News Digital on Thursday that the firing squad execution of convicted Fort Hood terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, allowing the public to witness the military's first execution in more than six decades.

"It will be livestreamed. Details will follow," a War Department official told Fox News Digital.

The execution is scheduled for Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, Texas.

FORT HOOD SURVIVOR SHOT IN HEAD VOWS TO WATCH TERRORIST FACE HISTORIC FIRING SQUAD

Hasan, a former Army major, killed 13 people and wounded 32 others when he opened fire on unarmed soldiers and civilians after shouting "Allahu Akbar" at Fort Hood on Nov. 5, 2009. He was convicted in 2013 and sentenced to death for the massacre.

President Donald Trump approved the use of an Army firing squad, following War Secretary Pete Hegseth's recommendation. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell previously announced the decision on X, declaring, "Judgment day for Hasan has finally come."

If carried out, Hasan's execution would be the first by the U.S. military since 1961 and the first military execution by firing squad since 1945. Hasan remains on military death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

item.title: Will Major League Baseball still lock players out after 2026 postseason proves owners wrong?
item.description: Major League Baseball's salary cap campaign takes a hit as four of the final five 2026 playoff teams rank in the bottom 11 in player payroll.
item.content:encoded:
Despite a number of fascinating storylines, much of the discussion during the 2026 Major League Baseball regular season was dominated by upcoming labor negotiations with the expiration of the Collective Bargaining Agreement in December.

The league office, essentially run by the 30 current owners, started an advertising and promotional campaign designed to inflame tensions and increase support for its proposed salary cap. As early as June, the league's official account made several posts telling fans how awful baseball is, while claiming that many fanbases have no "hope" of winning a World Series because of payroll disparities.

"The biggest issue baseball fans want solved to strengthen the game is fixing the payroll disparity that leaves too many fans without hope of their team competing for a World Series title," the first post said. "Every other major U.S. sport has tackled this problem, and every year more small market teams in those leagues have a chance to win. The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50."

MLB OWNERS REVEAL NEW DETAILS OF SALARY CAP PROPOSAL THAT ALL BUT GUARANTEE A LOCKOUT THIS DECEMBER

This was, of course, misleading; many teams get ancillary income that would not be included in the "50/50" split. And if the proposed floor would be achievable for the small market teams in 2027, it raises the question of why it wasn't in 2026. Even increased revenue sharing wouldn't come close to bridging the gap for most small market teams.

Regardless though, that "hope" section, again posted in June, has taken a major, major blow by the results in the postseason. Because it turns out that while spending helps, it doesn't guarantee results.

With the Dodgers, Brewers, and Tampa Bay Rays advancing to their respective league championship series on Wednesday, three of the four spots in the penultimate postseason round have been determined. The last spot will go to one of the Chicago White Sox or Cleveland Guardians. Five teams, out of 30, are left standing. Here's where they rank in pre-luxury tax player payroll in 2026, per Cot's Contracts:

The Dodgers are favorites to win the World Series, but as we've seen from years of experience, the favored team doesn't always win. And the Brewers will not be able to line up Jacob Misiorowski for two starts in the NLCS, including in Game 1 at American Family Field. Even if they do make it through the NLCS and the World Series, does the league really believe the message of "you have no hope" will resonate when four of the final five teams are in the bottom 11 in player payroll? Including the literal cheapest team in the sport, and coming off a series in which the No. 28 payroll team dominated the big spending Yankees in an easy 3-0 sweep?

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

These outcomes raise another key point; did Rays or White Sox fans realistically enter the season with "hope" of winning a World Series? Of course not. Chicago's just two seasons removed from one of the worst years in baseball history. The Rays did little this offseason to give fans reason for optimism. Yet here they are, favorites to advance through the American League for the second time in the past six years.

Milwaukee fans might have lost hope when the front office traded Freddy Peralta to the Mets in the offseason...only for the Brewers to have an even better record in 2026, the best win-loss and run differential in the sport. With the 19th highest payroll.

Point being, "hope" doesn't always relate to success. Mets fans started 2026 with "hope" after getting Peralta, Marcus Semien, Bo Bichette and Devin Williams. How'd that go? Yankees fans had hope with the exciting debut of Cam Schlittler in 2025, bringing back Cody Bellinger, and top prospects like Spencer Jones and George Lombard Jr., reaching the big leagues. Their reward? A sweep from the Rays.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Baseball isn't as predictable as it's made out to be, and injuries, prospects, underperformance and unexpected declines have a much greater impact than many want to admit.

Going back as far as 2010, it's clear that money helps, but competent front offices and smart money wins. Here are the most LCS appearances by organization starting that season

First, 22 of the 30 teams have reached the LCS since 2010, and if the White Sox advance with their 2-1 series lead, that'll grow to 23 of 30. Most small market teams have reached the LCS, many multiple times. Yes, the Dodgers have dominated, but the Mets have the same number of LCS appearances as Cleveland, Kansas City, and Tampa Bay. The Tigers have made it three times, as many as the Cubs or Red Sox. Should Cleveland advance, they'd join the list of teams with three appearances. Meanwhile, the huge market Los Angeles Angels haven't even reached the playoffs in the past decade.

Again, money absolutely matters. It clearly helps, the Dodgers are proof of that. But there are no guarantees in baseball, and LA's dominance is a testament to using their resources wisely. Obviously though, there's plenty of reason for hope for the vast majority of organizations, despite what the league's propaganda would lead you to believe.

item.description: Video shows a Delta passenger allegedly driving a stolen Alaska Airlines tug across the John Wayne Airport tarmac before crashing into another vehicle. The man was ultimately arrested.
item.content:encoded:
A traveler's reckless rampage with an airport tug created mayhem at a California airport Oct. 6.

Video from John Wayne Airport in Santa Ana shows a man behind the wheel of an airport tug on Tuesday, dangerously maneuvering around the airfield and, at one point, even reversing near a plane, according to Storyful.

Authorities identified the man as a 26-year-old from Everett, Washington. He had been scheduled to travel from John Wayne Airport to Seattle aboard a Delta Air Lines flight, according to FOX 59.

DRUNK MAN STEALS PLANE, SENDS FIGHTER JETS SCRAMBLING NEAR NUCLEAR PLANT

The incident began around 5:30 p.m., when the man allegedly gained access to the airfield through Gate 12, the outlet reported.

A Delta spokesperson told Fox News Digital the airline was cooperating with law enforcement after the unusual incident.

"Delta has zero tolerance for unlawful behavior, and we take all incidents seriously," a spokesperson said. 

"Nothing is more important than the safety and security of our customers and people, and we are cooperating fully with law enforcement."

After reaching the tarmac, the individual allegedly took an Alaska Airlines tug, one of the ground vehicles used around airports to move baggage and equipment, as FOX 59 reported.

Video footage shows the man driving the vehicle around the airfield and backing up near an aircraft.

"At approximately 5:30 p.m. Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, a Delta Airlines passenger breached gate 12 at the terminal and accessed the airfield," a spokesperson for John Wayne Airport told Fox News Digital.

"He stole an Alliance Ground International (AGI) baggage tug assigned to Alaska Airlines and crashed it into another vehicle by Gate 7. He attempted to steal an American Airlines lavatory truck and was arrested by Airport Police Services," the statement continued.

The man allegedly removed the restraints securing a Cessna 172 at Kalocsa Airport and took off in the aircraft before heading toward Paks, the home of Hungary's only nuclear power plant.

item.title: Caitlin Clark left off 19 WNBA MVP ballots despite historic season as A’ja Wilson wins fifth award
item.description: Caitlin Clark became the first WNBA player to average 20 points and eight assists in a season, yet 19 voters left her off MVP ballots entirely.
item.content:encoded:
Caitlin Clark received one first-place vote for WNBA MVP after producing a season nobody in the league had managed before.

And that might not even be the most ridiculous part of the results. Nineteen voters didn't put her on their ballots at all.

The WNBA announced Thursday that A’ja Wilson won her record fifth MVP award, receiving 65 of the 74 first-place votes from a panel of sportswriters and broadcasters. Minnesota rookie Olivia Miles finished second, followed by Indiana’s Kelsey Mitchell and Clark.

CAITLIN CLARK SAYS SHE BLOCKS SOCIAL MEDIA HATE AND ENJOYS HOSTILE WNBA ROAD CROWDS

Clark appeared on 55 ballots, receiving one first-place vote, six second-place votes, 20 third-place votes, 16 fourth-place votes and 12 fifth-place votes. She finished with 212 points, well behind Miles’ 442 and Mitchell’s 287.

Wilson had an outstanding season and a compelling case to win. But apparently, more than a quarter of the voters watched Clark this year and decided five other players deserved recognition ahead of her.

I'd love to hear those explanations.

Clark averaged 22.3 points and 8.3 assists per game, becoming the first WNBA player to finish a season averaging at least 20 points and eight assists.

Combining her own baskets and free throws with the points teammates scored from her assists, Clark created an average of 41.2 points per game. According to the WNBA’s own end-of-season review, that was the highest average in league history.

That's a useful place to start a conversation about offensive value, especially when her teammate finished ahead of her in MVP voting. There's a compelling case that Mitchell benefited from Clark far more than vice versa.

After all, Mitchell just completed her ninth WNBA season. In her six years with Indiana prior to Clark's arrival, Mitchell averaged 16.4 points per game. In the three seasons since the Fever drafted Clark, Mitchell has averaged 21.4 points, including a career-high 24.7 points this season.

Clark also had five games with at least 30 points and 10 assists this season. Every other player in WNBA history combined has four.

Read that again. Read that again. Caitlin Clark did something five times in one season that every other player combined has done four times in WNBA regular-season history.

Her best performance came against Seattle on July 17, when she scored 45 points and had 10 assists. It was the first 40-point, 10-assist game the WNBA had ever seen.

And those spectacular nights were backed by sustained production. Clark recorded 13 games with at least 20 points and 10 assists, nearly one-third of her 40 appearances. She finished with 891 points and 333 assists, becoming the first player to reach 800 points and 300 assists in a season.

Then there's the team success. Indiana averaged a league-record 96 points per game. Clark’s ability to score while creating opportunities for her teammates helped make that possible.

Apparently, some voters found all of that easier to overlook than others.

Miles averaged 19.8 points and six assists while helping Minnesota finish with the league’s best record. Although it's worth noting that Minnesota also finished with the league’s best record in 2025, before Miles entered the league.

Mitchell scored a league-record 1,086 points. That's impressive, but Clark helped create those scoring opportunities through both her passing and the defensive attention she draws.

Wilson, meanwhile, averaged 26.2 points and 9.4 rebounds, led the league in points and blocks per game, and helped Las Vegas win 31 games. Her ability to dominate at both ends gives voters plenty of reasons to put her first and, honestly, she probably deserved to win.

But choosing Wilson and leaving Clark outside the top five are very different judgments.

The award was decided by sportswriters and broadcasters. Given how some prominent members of that industry have covered Clark, skepticism about their judgment shouldn't surprise anyone.

Too much of the coverage treats her popularity as something that needs a racial explanation before anyone can simply appreciate her basketball.

In May, Cari Champion said about Clark: "I don’t like you. I don’t like the way you behave on the court."

By September, Champion was calling Clark an "avatar for people who want to spread hate."

In July, Nancy Armour argued that Clark’s reactions to officiating endangered Black and queer players, even invoking Emmett Till.

Even this week, Charlotte Wilder wanted "something a little more forceful" from Clark about the alleged treatment of Black WNBA players, despite acknowledging she had already spoken out.

That coverage reflects a preference for a story in which Black players need defending and Clark needs to constantly apologize for her mere existence. Her performance too often becomes secondary to what commentators believe her popularity represents.

Sportswriters, commentators and broadcasters are entitled to their opinions (as bad as they often are). Those examples don't tell us who left Clark off a ballot, but they help explain why fans might question the media’s judgment.

SOCIAL MEDIA WAS NOT LOVING CAITLIN CLARK GETTING SNUBBED BY TV NETWORK'S MVP GRAPHIC

And questioning their judgment doesn't require rooting against Wilson. She received only four Defensive Player of the Year votes while Angel Reese received 46 and won the award in a landslide.

I thought Wilson deserved considerably more support in that race, but as I argued at the time, the media loves to trumpet Reese as a star and they needed a reason to prop her up.

The standard should be consistent: evaluate what the players actually did, and be prepared to defend the result.

To be clear, Clark’s popularity doesn't entitle her to an MVP award. But it's not like her play didn't warrant consideration as the league's most valuable player.

There is room to disagree about how much weight to give defense, turnovers, scoring efficiency or a team’s record. Reasonable people can disagree about where Clark belonged behind Wilson, but leaving the Fever superstar outside the top five is borderline malpractice.

Nineteen voters decided a historic combination of scoring and playmaking wasn't worth even a fifth-place vote.

That doesn't prove that they simply don't like Caitlin Clark and don't want her to succeed, but it certainly raises the question.

If those 19 voters have a basketball explanation for leaving Clark off their ballots, they should make it public immediately.

item.title: Iranian protester hanged hours after marrying his imprisoned fiancée over jail phone line
item.description: Alireza Sepahi married his imprisoned fiancée over a prison phone line hours before his execution at Isfahan Central Prison for anti-government protest.
item.content:encoded:
An Iranian anti-regime protester was hanged at dawn Oct. 5 inside Isfahan Central Prison, just hours after marrying his imprisoned fiancée over a jail phone line, The Times reported Thursday.

Alireza Sepahi, 25, was executed alongside co-defendant Alireza Raisi after being sentenced to death in the anti-government demonstrations at Isfahan’s Alikhani Square Jan. 8., according to Human Rights Iran.

Sepahi and his bride, student activist Mahshad Keshani, 22, knew and loved each other before being arrested during anti-regime demonstrations, the report said.

IRAN HANGS 2 PROTESTERS IN PUBLIC, CROWD CRIES 'DISHONORABLE' AS SECURITY FIRES TEAR GAS

Keshani, who is serving a five-year sentence, pushed for an informal wedding Sunday as fears mounted that Sepahi’s execution was imminent after a final family summons.

The couple exchanged vows over the phone from inside Isfahan prison, joined by their fathers.

Human rights lawyer Amirsalar Davoudi facilitated the ceremony by reading the vows for the fathers to bless.

Keshani’s family gave a copy of the Quran, a saffron rock candy and a single red rose as a traditional dowry.

"It was Mahshad’s idea," Davoudi told The Times. "Even now, I wonder how one young woman can possess such courage."

IRAN TO EXECUTE FIRST FEMALE PROTESTER TIED TO ANTI-REGIME UNREST

Davoudi recalled warning Keshani about the permanent nature of the decision. 

"I told her, ‘My dear, you understand that this cannot simply be undone?’" Davoudi said. 

"She said, ‘Mr Davoudi, I love Alireza.’"

When Davoudi presented the proposal to Sepahi, the young man broke down in tears. 

"Alireza was crying, and something deeply painful and beautiful happened. Even the prison officers began to cry," Davoudi said.

The ceremony held no formal authority to halt the execution. Sepahi had previously survived a scheduled hanging in July after suffering a heart attack on his way to the gallows. Authorities then rescheduled the execution after he regained consciousness.

On Monday morning, hours after the vows were spoken, Sepahi was hanged.

IRAN'S REGIME CAME FOR TEENAGE TWINS. THEIR FATE OFFERS A GLIMPSE OF TEHRAN'S WIDENING DEATH CAMPAIGN

He is among seven defendants executed in the Alikhani Square case, in which 12 men were accused in the deaths of four security personnel.

After the hanging, Sepahi’s family was reportedly prevented by authorities from burying their son in his hometown.

Davoudi condemned the Iranian regime's actions. 

"I do not know how to come to terms with this," Davoudi said.

"The regime is taking revenge on innocent young people for the humiliation it has suffered internationally."

Human rights groups report Keshani remains in custody, facing additional security charges.

This came as Maryam Rajavi, president-elect of the National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI), urged U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres to take immediate international action to halt executions and the killing of protesters in Iran, citing thousands of executions and decades of impunity for human rights abuses. 

In a letter ahead of World Day Against the Death Penalty on Oct. 10, Rajavi called for international accountability, independent investigations and diplomatic and economic pressure on Tehran to end the executions.

item.title: World Series champion Ryan Howard details why coaching and accountability set the tone for winning
item.description: Philadelphia Phillies legend Ryan Howard told OutKick in a recent interview that a team's clubhouse chemistry is integral to a team's success.
item.content:encoded:
For Major League Baseball teams, a team's culture and chemistry is paramount to gutting through the grueling season - and according to World Series champion Ryan Howard, it outweighs a team's talent.

MLB plays 162 regular-season games in about 180 days, from the end of March until the beginning of October. Spring training starts in the middle of February, and if a team makes a deep postseason run, the season may not end until the end of October.

During the long and arduous season, players see each other more than they see their families. Philadelphia Phillies legend Ryan Howard told OutKick that a strong clubhouse culture and team chemistry outweigh the team’s talent.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Every team has talent, but I always say if you have the culture and chemistry. That culture and chemistry will outweigh talent, any day. To where you put the two together, you're unstoppable," Howard told OutKick in a recent interview.

Howard, who spent his entire 13-year career with the Phillies, said it was the coaches who established the clubhouse’s culture.

"I think for us, it started from the top with the coaching staff. When you have coaches that give you a positive environment every single day that you show up, it's loose, it's lax, you've got coaches that you know are gonna go and they're gonna fight for you, no matter what, on the field, off the field. You create that environment and it makes it easier for the players to all want to be able to get along," Howard said.

"When you have people that have the mindset of, hey, we want to win, not want to win, we expect to win. So, when everybody shows up with that mindset, day in and day out, you know the work that's gonna need to go in and your coaching staff is helping to continue to grow that environment, man, it makes it so easy."

The 2006 NL MVP said that when the coaches put in the same amount of work, if not more, than the players do to help them become the best they can possibly be, you can’t ask for anything more as a player. In addition to helping everyone become the best players they could be, Howard pointed to the coaching staff holding players accountable as a critical part of a good clubhouse.

The three-time All-Star recalled a time when one of his managers pulled shortstop Jimmy Rollins from a game due to a lack of effort.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"The manager had to get on my man, young James, Jimmy Rollins, for not running out a fly ball, taking him out of the game. For hitting a pop fly and not running hard down to first base or something like that," Howard said.

Howard said that in a good clubhouse, coaches aren’t the only ones holding players accountable; the players do so as well. Howard said that on one occasion, Rollins got on outfielder Shane Victorino for jogging after a fly ball.

"It's one of those things where it's like, all it took is that one time for you to tell me. And I got it. And then the next play, it's like, all right, you're sprinting after the ball or you're sprinting out of the box, you're doing it, all it takes is one time because as you said, it's a long season. So sometimes you're gonna have those little mental lulls and all that stuff," Howard said.

"But when you can have the people there to kind of help keep you accountable, again, all it takes is that one time or that that one kick in the butt just to kind of get you back on track and then you're back moving where we need you to go."

The Phillies were eliminated by the Atlanta Braves last week in the National League Wild Card Series, and the future looks bleak.

After making the World Series in 2022, they have regressed year after year. In 2023, they lost in the NLCS, lost in the NLDS in 2024 and 2025, and now in the Wild Card round this season.

Since 2022, the team has maintained the same core but has still not managed to get over the hump and win a World Series title. The issue for the Phillies is that the core of first baseman Bryce Harper (33), designated hitter Kyle Schwarber (33), shortstop Trea Turner (33), catcher J.T. Realmuto (35), starting pitchers Zack Wheeler (36), Aaron Nola (33), Jesús Luzardo (29) and Cristopher Sánchez (29) is only getting older.

Howard was in a similar situation later in his career.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

"It's interesting because having been somewhat in that position where teams I was on, it's like, hey, at some point, your team continues to age, and you continue to get older, and it's like, when do you hold on?" Howard said.

He cited the length of many of the core players’ contracts as an issue for the team because they are harder to move in a trade. Harper’s deal runs through 2031, Schwarber’s through 2030, Turner’s through 2033, Realmuto’s through 2028, Wheeler’s through 2027, Nola’s through 2030, Luzardo’s through 2031 and Sánchez’s through 2032.

Compounding the Phillies’ problems, their farm system was ranked 26th in the sport by MLB.com, meaning there aren’t any immediate options to supplant struggling stars. Howard said something has to change for the Phillies, whether players are moved or not.

"If you can't necessarily move people, then what you gotta do is, is you gotta change. To me, I think you got to change the philosophy and the dynamic inside the clubhouse. 'Cause if they're not going anywhere, then you've got to switch something up that you're doing internally. You know, I don't know whether that's a playing style. I don't, I don't know what that is. I don't know what that is," Howard said.

"If you're going to continue to have the same squad, then you're going to have to internally as an organization, as a team, have to say, ‘Hey, we're gonna have to either play a different brand of ball, or we're gonna have to do this ’ or kind of figure something else out and mix it up, because what's been going on obviously hasn't worked in the in the previous few seasons."

Howard, who is on the Phillies Wall of Fame, said he couldn’t thank all of the coaches, from T-ball to the big leagues, enough for helping him get to where he was in his career. One coach who had a major impact on Howard was assistant hitting coach Ali Modami.

The St. Louis native said Modami was integral to his preparation heading into each game.

"I would run down to the cage, get my man Ali down there, and we would work our routine, starting on the tees, starting our flips, doing all this, doing all that. I would ask him to, hey, work me this way today. Let's try to do this approach today because this is the approach that I may want to try to take into the game against this pitcher today," Howard, who spoke on behalf of PAYDAY to highlight the low-key legends who helped shape his career, said.

item.title: ABC News deletes ‘hit piece’ on Trump sons' Pentagon-linked investments without explanation
item.description: ABC News quietly deleted its report on Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump's alleged ties to Pentagon contracts after 1789 Capital threatened legal action.
item.content:encoded:
ABC News deleted a report criticizing the business dealings of President Donald Trump’s oldest sons, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, Thursday after facing legal threats but has failed to provide any explanation or editor’s note for the vanished "hit piece."

The now-deleted report, which can still be viewed via the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine, was published Wednesday with the headline, "Trump sons' investments have won billions in Pentagon contracts since his election," and said Anduril, the company investing in a new Baltimore shipyard, had ties to Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump.

"1789 Capital — a venture capital firm that lists Donald Trump Jr. as one of six partners along with three founders — claimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company," ABC News reported in the deleted story.

TRUMP TURNS TO EMERGING TECH GIANT IN MULTI-BILLION BID TO RAMP UP US SUBMARINE PRODUCTION

"Since that investment, Anduril has been awarded 135 other contracts with the U.S. government and to date has received around $1.8 billion from those agreements, according to active defense contracts posted to SAM.gov, the official system for government contracting. 

"The company is one of the largest manufacturers to receive an investment from Donald Trump Jr. and his brother Eric Trump, but they are not the only one."

Alexa Henning, a spokesperson for 1789 Capital and a former chief of staff to the director of national intelligence, took to social media, insisting the company does not have a "major stake" in Anduril and blasting the "biased hit piece."

"Here's a small lesson, that I also explained to ABC, the ‘reporter’ who is a complete idiot conflated raising funds with investment by 1789. Those are two separate actions," Henning wrote.

"Meaning the ‘investments’ mentioned were actually the total number raised for a funding round, that MANY companies contribute to," Henning continued. 

"Another thing that the reporter buried the lead on was that many of these companies have gotten government contracts during Biden AND Trump, which completely negates the assertion by ABC that Don Jr and Eric Trump are doing anything wrong."

JARED KUSHNER SCOLDS CNN OVER 'DEEPLY MISLEADING’ REPORT, SAYS KEY INFO BURIED BEHIND PAYWALL

Shortly after, ABC News deleted the story from its website. The link to the original report now states, "This page either does not exist or is currently unavailable."

ABC News did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The network has not issued a correction or provided a public explanation for why the report was removed from its website.

ABC News also deleted a viral X post intended to promote the story that was shared by several prominent Democrats.

Henning spoke to Fox News Digital after ABC News deleted the story. She said that in addition to calling out the story publicly on X, she sent a detailed email to ABC News pointing out mistakes in the reporting and informing the Disney-owned network that lawyers would be in touch if action was not taken.

She said she "really appreciates that they took it down" but wants a clear explanation of why it was published in the first place and believes ABC News should inform readers of its errors.

‘LIBELOUS’ NYT REPORT TYING TRUMP FAMILY TO GOVERNMENT-BACKED DEAL SPARKS LEGAL DEMAND

Henning also told Fox News Digital that ABC News never asked 1789 Capital for comment prior to the story’s initial publication despite being mentioned several times in the initial report.

"The majority of people reporting on 1789 do not fundamentally understand how it works," she said. 

Once the story had vanished, Trump Jr. responded to California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who had shared the initial ABC News report on X.

"ABC deleted this article in less than 24 hours because it’s false. Sounds about as long as your presidential campaign would last," Trump Jr. wrote.

Fox News Digital’s Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

item.title: Liberty make official inquiry into reset timeout dispute after overtime loss to Dream in WNBA semifinals
item.description: Breanna Stewart says officials told the Liberty they had no reset timeout when they actually did, sparking an inquiry after Atlanta Dream's OT win.
item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Dream moved within one victory of a WNBA Finals berth after outlasting the New York Liberty 101-98 in overtime Wednesday night to take a commanding 2-0 lead in the semifinal series.

However, Game 2’s dramatic finish was overshadowed by controversy after New York star Breanna Stewart said officials incorrectly told the Liberty they did not have a reset timeout available in the closing seconds, even though the team still had one remaining.

"This is not blaming the refs, but when I ask both refs if we have a reset timeout at the end, and they tell us no, and then we leave the game with the reset timeout, it's pretty frustrating," Stewart told reporters after the game.

DREAM MOVE WITHIN ONE WIN OF FIRST WNBA FINALS APPEARANCE SINCE 2013 AFTER OVERTIME VICTORY

Under league rules, each team is given two team timeouts and one reset timeout during overtime, allowing it to advance the ball without huddling on the sideline.

Stewart continued later: "I asked Kevin [Fahy]. I said, 'Do we have a reset timeout?' And he said, 'I'm going to check at the table.' So then he looked to [crew chief] Fatou [Cissoko-Stephens], and she said, 'No.' So then he told me, 'No.'"

A late New York turnover gave Atlanta an opportunity to put the game away. Angel Reese, the 2026 WNBA Defensive Player of the Year, went to the foul line and sank both free throws to extend the Dream’s lead to three points. The Liberty inbounded from under their own basket and got the ball to Stewart, but her desperation shot was no good as the clock ticked to triple zeros.

WNBA'S OFFICIATING OVERHAUL IS ALREADY DRAWING COMPLAINTS FROM PLAYERS AND COACHES ONE WEEK INTO SEASON

"Of course, who knows what happened to end the game," Stewart said. "But we would have had hopefully a better shot on our goal."

Officials were not made available to members of the media until roughly two hours after the game. ESPN asked crew chief Fatou Cissoko-Stephens in the pool report why Stewart said she had been told the Liberty's reset timeout wasn't available.

"Stewart was standing behind referee Fahy when he confirmed with his partner between Reese's penalty free throws that New York did indeed have a reset timeout remaining," she said.

The controversy has prompted the Liberty to formally inquire with the league about the situation, ESPN reported, citing sources.

Asked whether he was unaware that the team had a reset timeout at their disposal, Liberty coach Chris DeMarco responded, "Yeah, same thing. They just said we didn't have it. Multiple staff members [were told]. It is what it is. We've got to demand more. But it is what it is."

Dream coach Karl Smesko was also asked about the number of Liberty timeouts remaining.

"I was, I thought they had a timeout left," Smesko said. "But they played it out the way they did. So I was expecting it to be advanced, but it wasn't, so we had to play it, and fortunately we were able to get the stop."

Cissoko-Stephens added that the scorer’s table and stats staff keep up with the number of available timeouts, but emphasized that "teams are responsible for managing and tracking their timeout usage throughout the game."

When the Liberty had possession in critical moments, they failed to capitalize on their opportunities. With less than 10 seconds remaining in overtime, Ionescu lost control of the ball while driving, sending it out of bounds. Ionescu took responsibility for the costly mistake.

"I told them it was my fault," she said. "I took ownership for that. This loss is on me. I've got to take it on the chin, and I've got to be better."

Atlanta’s depth was on full display as six players scored in double figures, led by Reese and Jordin Canada with 23 points apiece. The Dream's leading scorer Allisha Gray sat out of the game due to a finger injury.

The Liberty would have to overcome unprecedented odds to become the first team in WNBA history to erase a 2-0 deficit and win a best-of-five playoff series. Game 3 is scheduled for Friday night as the series shifts to Brooklyn, New York.

item.title: Glen Powell wants no part of political fights that divide people
item.description: Glen Powell says political discourse is "the worst version of a conversation" and reveals how movies remain his preferred way to express himself.
item.content:encoded:
Glen Powell wants nothing to do with Hollywood's political firestorms.

The "Top Gun: Maverick" star opened up about his decision to stay out of politics and why he believes the growing divide has made it nearly impossible to have a healthy conversation.

"Over time, I realized that politics divide people," Powell told Esquire. "People trying to prove their point – for me, it’s the worst version of a conversation. I genuinely do not like the discourse. It’s not as healthy as it once was."

DWAYNE 'THE ROCK' JOHNSON REJECTS HOLLYWOOD’S POLITICAL OBSESSION, BLASTS CELEBRITY ATTACK CULTURE

For Powell, engaging in politics is "not presently possible."

"I applaud people for jumping into those things and fighting for what they believe in," he added. "If I were a political person, I would be talking about it. For me, my calling is elsewhere."

Powell's reluctance to wade into politics dates back to his upbringing.

Despite his mother's work in the Reagan administration at the U.S. Treasury Department, the actor said politics and current events weren't regular topics of conversation around the family dinner table.

He echoed the sentiment in a previous interview with The Guardian.

"I’m not a political person," he said in October 2025. "I like things that bring people together."

DOLLY PARTON REFUSED TO PICK POLITICAL SIDES FOR DECADES: ‘I’M NOT IN POLITICS, I’M AN ENTERTAINER’

With politics increasingly dividing audiences, even Hollywood's biggest stars are finding it harder to appeal to everyone. Powell weighed in on whether entertainment can still bring Americans together and if action movies are one of the last remaining escapes from the political divide.

"That’s a good point. There’s a universal language of action, which is also why those movies translate so well internationally," he added. "'Running Man' is about something universal – what you would be willing to do for the people you love? But also how people can feel powerless in the face of a world that feels more and more unequal, more unfair."

"So, you’re not going to see me talk politics. But movies – that’s how I express myself," he added. "Movies are a conversation; politics always felt to me like two people trying to prove a point."

Powell has become one of Hollywood's most recognizable leading men, thanks to standout performances in "Top Gun: Maverick," "Anyone But You" and "Twisters."

Yet his stardom didn't light overnight.

He once had a casting director tell him he'd be lucky to "play a dead body" on CSI as he struggled for a decade to get his foot in the door.

"There was a point where I realized that acting is not a meritocracy," he said during an appearance on "CBS Mornings." And just because you exist on a longer timeline doesn't mean it's going to work out. Right? There's a lot of other bigger forces at play."

"The fact that all of those sort of detours along the way about learning how to sort of develop and raise money and write – all these things are now kind of leading me to a place where all of those weapons are at my disposal," he added.

The Hollywood heartthrob kept his hot streak alive in 2026, starring alongside Margaret Qualley in the dark comedy thriller "How to Make a Killing" before lending his voice to Fox McCloud in "The Super Mario Galaxy Movie."

The Texas-born star is gearing up for two major 2027 projects, including Judd Apatow's comedy "The Comeback King" and J.J. Abrams' sci-fi adventure "The Great Beyond."
